statement: Disquisitiones Arithmeticae (Latin for Arithmetical Investigations) is a textbook on number theory written in Latin by Carl Friedrich Gauss in 1798, when Gauss was 21, and published in 1801, when he was 24.

subject: Disquisitiones Arithmeticae
statement: It had a revolutionary impact on number theory by making the field truly rigorous and systematic and paved the path for modern number theory.

subject: Disquisitiones Arithmeticae
statement: In this book, Gauss brought together and reconciled results in number theory obtained by such eminent mathematicians as Fermat, Euler, Lagrange, and Legendre, while adding profound and original results of his own.

subject: Disquisitiones Arithmeticae
statement: Scope The Disquisitiones covers both elementary number theory and parts of the area of mathematics now called algebraic number theory.

subject: Disquisitiones Arithmeticae
statement: Gauss did not explicitly recognize the concept of a group, which is central to modern algebra, so he did not use this term.

subject: Disquisitiones Arithmeticae
statement: His own title for his subject was Higher Arithmetic.

subject: Disquisitiones Arithmeticae
statement: In his Preface to the Disquisitiones, Gauss describes the scope of the book as follows: The inquiries which this volume will investigate pertain to that part of Mathematics which concerns itself with integers.

subject: Disquisitiones Arithmeticae
statement: Gauss also writes, "When confronting many difficult problems, derivations have been suppressed for the sake of brevity when readers refer to this work." ("Quod, in pluribus quaestionibus difficilibus, demonstrationibus syntheticis usus sum, analysinque per quam erutae sunt suppressi, imprimis brevitatis studio tribuendum est, cui quantum fieri poterat consulere oportebat.") Contents The book is divided into seven sections: Congruent Numbers in General Congruences of the First Degree Residues of Powers Congruences of the Second Degree Forms and Indeterminate Equations of the Second Degree Various Applications of the Preceding Discussions Equations Defining Sections of a Circle These sections are subdivided into 366 numbered items, which state a theorem with proof or otherwise develop a remark or thought.

subject: Disquisitiones Arithmeticae
statement: Sections I to III are essentially a review of previous results, including Fermat's little theorem, Wilson's theorem and the existence of primitive roots.

subject: Disquisitiones Arithmeticae
statement: Although few of the results in these sections are original, Gauss was the first mathematician to bring this material together in a systematic way.

subject: Disquisitiones Arithmeticae
statement: He also realized the importance of the property of unique factorization (assured by the fundamental theorem of arithmetic, first studied by Euclid), which he restates and proves using modern tools.

subject: Disquisitiones Arithmeticae
statement: From Section IV onward, much of the work is original.

subject: Disquisitiones Arithmeticae
statement: Section IV develops a proof of quadratic reciprocity; Section V, which takes up over half of the book, is a comprehensive analysis of binary and ternary quadratic forms.

subject: Disquisitiones Arithmeticae
statement: Section VI includes two different primality tests.

subject: Disquisitiones Arithmeticae
statement: Finally, Section VII is an analysis of cyclotomic polynomials, which concludes by giving the criteria that determine which regular polygons are constructible, i.e., can be constructed with a compass and unmarked straightedge alone.

subject: Disquisitiones Arithmeticae
statement: Gauss started to write an eighth section on higher-order congruences, but did not complete it, and it was published separately after his death with the title Disquisitiones generales de congruentiis (Latin: 'General Investigations on Congruences').

subject: Disquisitiones Arithmeticae
statement: In it Gauss discussed congruences of arbitrary degree, attacking the problem of general congruences from a standpoint closely related to that taken later by Dedekind, Galois, and Emil Artin.

subject: Disquisitiones Arithmeticae
statement: The treatise paved the way for the theory of function fields over a finite field of constants.

subject: Disquisitiones Arithmeticae
statement: Ideas unique to that treatise are clear recognition of the importance of the Frobenius morphism, and a version of Hensel's lemma.

subject: Disquisitiones Arithmeticae
statement: The Disquisitiones was one of the last mathematical works written in scholarly Latin.

subject: Distance
statement: Distance is a numerical or occasionally qualitative measurement of how far apart objects, points, people, or ideas are.

subject: Distance
statement: In physics or everyday usage, distance may refer to a physical length or an estimation based on other criteria (e.g.

subject: Distance
statement: The term is also frequently used metaphorically to mean a measurement of the amount of difference between two similar objects (such as statistical distance between probability distributions or edit distance between strings of text) or a degree of separation (as exemplified by distance between people in a social network).

subject: Distance
statement: Most such notions of distance, both physical and metaphorical, are formalized in mathematics using the notion of a metric space.

subject: Distance
statement: In the social sciences, distance can refer to a qualitative measurement of separation, such as social distance or psychological distance.

subject: Distance
statement: Distances in physics and geometry The distance between physical locations can be defined in different ways in different contexts.

subject: Distance
object: length of a straight line between them
statement: Straight-line or Euclidean distance The distance between two points in physical space is the length of a straight line between them, which is the shortest possible path.

subject: Distance
statement: This is the usual meaning of distance in classical physics, including Newtonian mechanics.

subject: Distance
statement: Straight-line distance is formalized mathematically as the Euclidean distance in two- and three-dimensional space.

subject: Distance
statement: In Euclidean geometry, the distance between two points A and B is often denoted | A B | {\displaystyle |AB|} .

subject: Distance
statement: In coordinate geometry, Euclidean distance is computed using the Pythagorean theorem.

subject: Distance
statement: The distance between points (x1, y1) and (x2, y2) in the plane is given by: d ( Δ x ) 2 + ( Δ y ) 2 ( x 2 − x 1 ) 2 + ( y 2 − y 1 ) 2 .

subject: Distance
statement: {\displaystyle d {\sqrt {(\Delta x)^{2}+(\Delta y)^{2}}} {\sqrt {(x_{2}-x_{1})^{2}+(y_{2}-y_{1})^{2}}}.} Similarly, given points (x1, y1, z1) and (x2, y2, z2) in three-dimensional space, the distance between them is: d ( Δ x ) 2 + ( Δ y ) 2 + ( Δ z ) 2 ( x 2 − x 1 ) 2 + ( y 2 − y 1 ) 2 + ( z 2 − z 1 ) 2 .

subject: Distance
statement: {\displaystyle d {\sqrt {(\Delta x)^{2}+(\Delta y)^{2}+(\Delta z)^{2}}} {\sqrt {(x_{2}-x_{1})^{2}+(y_{2}-y_{1})^{2}+(z_{2}-z_{1})^{2}}}.} This idea generalizes to higher-dimensional Euclidean spaces.

subject: Distance
statement: Measurement There are many ways of measuring straight-line distances.

subject: Distance
statement: For example, it can be done directly using a ruler, or indirectly with a radar (for long distances) or interferometry (for very short distances).

subject: Distance
statement: The cosmic distance ladder is a set of ways of measuring extremely long distances.

subject: Distance
statement: Shortest-path distance on a curved surface The straight-line distance between two points on the surface of the Earth is not very useful for most purposes, since we cannot tunnel straight through the Earth's mantle.

subject: Distance
statement: Instead, one typically measures the shortest path along the surface of the Earth, as the crow flies.

subject: Distance
statement: This is approximated mathematically by the great-circle distance on a sphere.

subject: Division (mathematics)
statement: Division is one of the four basic operations of arithmetic.

subject: Division (mathematics)
statement: The other operations are addition, subtraction, and multiplication.

subject: Division (mathematics)
statement: What is being divided is called the dividend, which is divided by the divisor, and the result is called the quotient.

subject: Division (mathematics)
statement: At an elementary level the division of two natural numbers is, among other possible interpretations, the process of calculating the number of times one number is contained within another.

subject: Division (mathematics)
statement: For example, if 20 apples are divided evenly between 4 people, everyone receives 5 apples (see picture).

subject: Division (mathematics)
object: number of times the second number is completely contained in the first number
statement: The division with remainder or Euclidean division of two natural numbers provides an integer quotient, which is the number of times the second number is completely contained in the first number, and a remainder, which is the part of the first number that remains, when in the course of computing the quotient, no further full chunk of the size of the second number can be allocated.

subject: Division (mathematics)
statement: For example, if 21 apples are divided between 4 people, everyone receives 5 apples, and 1 apple remains.

subject: Division (mathematics)
statement: For division to always yield one number rather than a quotient and a remainder, the natural numbers must be extended to rational numbers or real numbers.

subject: Division (mathematics)
statement: In these enlarged number systems, division is the inverse operation to multiplication, that is a c / b means a × b c, as long as b is not zero; division by zero is not defined.

subject: Division (mathematics)
statement: In the 21-apples example, everyone would receive 5 apples and a quarter of an apple, with none left over.

subject: Division (mathematics)
statement: Both forms of division appear in various algebraic structures, different ways of defining mathematical structure.

subject: Division (mathematics)
statement: Those in which a Euclidean division (with remainder) is defined are called Euclidean domains and include polynomial rings in one indeterminate (which define multiplication and addition over single-variabled formulas).

subject: Division (mathematics)
statement: Those in which a division (with a single result) by all nonzero elements is defined are called fields and division rings.

subject: Division (mathematics)
statement: In a ring the elements by which division is always possible are called the units (for example, 1 and −1 in the ring of integers).

subject: Division (mathematics)
statement: Another generalization of division to algebraic structures is the quotient group, in which the result of "division" is a group rather than a number.

subject: Division (mathematics)
statement: Introduction The simplest way of viewing division is in terms of quotition and partition: from the quotition perspective, 20 / 5 means the number of 5s that must be added to get 20.

subject: Division (mathematics)
statement: In terms of partition, 20 / 5 means the size of each of 5 parts into which a set of size 20 is divided.

subject: Division (mathematics)
statement: For example, 20 apples divide into five groups of four apples, meaning that "twenty divided by five is equal to four".

subject: Division (mathematics)
statement: This is denoted as 20 / 5 4, or ⁠20/5⁠ 4.

subject: Division (mathematics)
statement: In the example, 20 is the dividend, 5 is the divisor, and 4 is the quotient.

subject: Doctor of Philosophy
statement: A Doctor of Philosophy (PhD, DPhil; Latin: philosophiae doctor or doctor in philosophia) is a terminal degree that usually denotes the highest level of academic achievement in a given discipline and is awarded following a course of graduate study and original research.

subject: Doctor of Philosophy
statement: The name of the degree is most often abbreviated PhD (or, at times, as Ph.D.

subject: Doctor of Philosophy
statement: in North America) and is pronounced as three separate letters ( PEE-aych-DEE).

subject: Doctor of Philosophy
statement: The University of Oxford uses the alternative abbreviation "DPhil".

subject: Doctor of Philosophy
statement: PhDs are awarded for programs across the whole breadth of academic fields.

subject: Doctor of Philosophy
statement: Since it is an earned research degree, those studying for a PhD are required to produce original research that expands the boundaries of knowledge, normally in the form of a dissertation, and, in some cases, defend their work before a panel of other experts in the field.

subject: Doctor of Philosophy
statement: In many fields, the completion of a PhD is typically required for employment as a university professor, researcher, or scientist.

subject: Doctor of Philosophy
statement: Definition In the context of the Doctor of Philosophy and other similarly titled degrees, the term "philosophy" does not refer to the field or academic discipline of philosophy, but is used in a broader sense in accordance with its original Greek meaning, which is "love of wisdom".

subject: Doctor of Philosophy
statement: In most of Europe, all fields (including history, philosophy, social sciences, mathematics, and natural philosophy – later known as natural science) other than theology, law, and medicine (the so-called professional, vocational, or technical curricula) were traditionally known as philosophy, and in Germany and elsewhere in Europe the basic faculty of liberal arts was known as the "faculty of philosophy".

subject: Doctor of Philosophy
statement: A PhD candidate must submit a project, thesis, or dissertation often consisting of a body of original academic research, which is in principle worthy of publication in a peer-reviewed journal.

subject: Doctor of Philosophy
statement: In many countries, a candidate must defend this work before a panel of expert examiners appointed by the university.

subject: Doctor of Philosophy
statement: Universities sometimes award other types of doctorate besides the PhD, such as the Doctor of Musical Arts (DMA) for music performers, Doctor of Juridical Science (SJD) for legal scholars and the Doctor of Education (EdD) for studies in education.

subject: Doctor of Philosophy
statement: In 2005 the European University Association defined the "Salzburg Principles", 10 basic principles for third-cycle degrees (doctorates) within the Bologna Process.

subject: Doctor of Philosophy
statement: These were followed in 2016 by the "Florence Principles", seven basic principles for doctorates in the arts laid out by the European League of Institutes of the Arts, which have been endorsed by the European Association of Conservatoires, the International Association of Film and Television Schools, the International Association of Universities and Colleges of Art, Design and Media, and the Society for Artistic Research.The specific requirements to earn a PhD degree vary considerably according to the country, institution, and time period, from entry-level research degrees to higher doctorates.

subject: Doctor of Philosophy
statement: During the studies that lead to the degree, the student is called a doctoral student or PhD student; a student who has completed any necessary coursework and related examinations and is working on their thesis/dissertation is sometimes known as a doctoral candidate or PhD candidate.

subject: Doctor of Philosophy
statement: A student attaining this level may be granted a Candidate of Philosophy degree at some institutions or may be granted a master's degree en route to the doctoral degree.

subject: Doctor of Philosophy
statement: Sometimes this status is also colloquially known as "ABD", meaning "all but dissertation".

subject: Doctor of Philosophy
statement: PhD graduates may undertake a postdoc in the process of transitioning from study to academic tenure.

subject: Doctor of Philosophy
statement: Individuals who have earned the Doctor of Philosophy degree use the title Doctor (often abbreviated "Dr" or "Dr."), although the etiquette associated with this usage may be subject to the professional ethics of the particular scholarly field, culture, or society.

subject: Doctor of Philosophy
statement: Those who teach at universities or work in academic, educational, or research fields are usually addressed by this title "professionally and socially in a salutation or conversation".
